article.title: Veterans, Labor, and the Fight to Save the VA From Privatization
article.author: Steve Early
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At a time when federal workers face mounting attacks on their jobs, collective bargaining rights, and public services, a growing coalition of veterans and labor activists is working to defend one of America's most important public institutions: the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). That struggle was the focus of How Veterans in Labor Are Fighting Trump, VA Privatization, & Union Busting , a discussion at the 4th Annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at Cal State LA. The session featured Eric Goepel , an Army veteran, Communications Workers of America (CWA) Local 6251 member, and Southern California organizer for Common Defense, a progressive veterans organization. Steve Early , longtime labor journalist, union activist, and co-author of Courage or Complicity: How Veterans Are Responding to the Attack on Democracy , moderated the discussion. Their central argument was that veterans possess an often-overlooked source of political power: their presence within organized labor and their capacity to mobilize across traditional political divisions. Veterans in Labor Are Fighting Trump (1:07:32) Veterans Are an Untapped Force in Organized Labor Early emphasized that approximately one million former military service members belong to labor unions, yet relatively few unions systematically identify, organize, or develop these members as activists. He argued that unions have historically underestimated veterans' potential as organizers, even though military veterans have played important roles in some of America's most consequential labor struggles. From the Teamsters' reform movement to battles against corrupt union leadership, veterans have repeatedly demonstrated their willingness to challenge powerful institutions. Early suggested that unions should establish networks of veteran shop stewards, local officers, and rank-and-file members, providing political education and leadership training that connects workplace struggles with broader campaigns for social justice. Goepel agreed, describing veteran organizing as a potential "force multiplier." When veterans receive training and opportunities to organize within their existing communities, their influence can extend far beyond individual membership. With millions of workers represented by AFL-CIO unions, the organizational infrastructure already exists to make veteran activism a significant force within the labor movement. The missing ingredient, both speakers suggested, is sustained commitment. Related: ICE Killing in Maine Shows Why Vets Need Vetting—And Not Just in Politics The Fight Against VA Privatization Goepel described Common Defense's campaign, "VA Not for Sale," which challenges the growing diversion of veterans' healthcare funding into private medical systems. Over the past two decades, federal policies have increasingly expanded the use of private-sector providers through the VA's community care programs. Goepel argued that these policies threaten to weaken the public healthcare system by transferring resources away from VA facilities already struggling with staffing shortages. But the problem reaches beyond veterans. The VA is also a major training institution for America's healthcare workforce. Physicians, nurses, medical researchers, and other professionals gain valuable experience through its hospitals and affiliated medical centers. Weakening the VA, Goepel argued, therefore threatens the broader healthcare system. His proposed response involves restoring staffing, rebuilding institutional capacity, and reversing policies that encourage privatization rather than strengthening public services. The objective is not simply preserving existing programs. It is demonstrating that publicly provided healthcare can deliver high-quality services without making private profits its organizing principle. Why Veterans' Benefits Should Inform Healthcare for Everyone One of Goepel's most significant observations concerned the contradiction between America's treatment of veterans and its treatment of the broader population. Veterans have access to a network of public benefits involving healthcare, education, housing assistance, disability compensation, and employment support. Although these systems have serious shortcomings and inequalities, Goepel argued that they demonstrate something important: government can establish comprehensive programs intended to meet essential human needs. Why, he asked, should comparable protections remain unavailable to millions of other Americans? He pointed to military toxic exposure as another example. Veterans harmed by burn pits and other hazardous conditions have won expanded recognition and benefits through federal legislation. Yet civilians living near contaminated military installations may face similar environmental consequences without equivalent protections. For Goepel, defending veterans' benefits and expanding social rights are not competing objectives. They are connected struggles. Related: Not Every Veteran Candidate Is a Champion for Veterans Confronting the Military-Industrial Complex The discussion eventually moved beyond VA privatization to the enormous federal resources devoted to military spending. Participants questioned why Washington continues expanding military budgets while threatening cuts to healthcare, education, housing, and other public services. Goepel acknowledged a difficult contradiction: military contracting supports many well-paying union jobs. Workers employed by defense contractors cannot reasonably be expected to embrace reductions in weapons production without credible alternatives for their livelihoods. Early pointed to the concept of economic conversion , an approach advocated by labor reformers for decades. Rather than simply eliminating military production jobs, economic conversion would redirect industrial capacity toward civilian needs while protecting workers' wages, benefits, and employment opportunities. Factories producing military equipment, for example, could be redirected toward infrastructure, public transportation, or other socially useful production. Both speakers argued that such a transition requires government investment and planning, not abandonment of affected workers. The issue is ultimately one of national priorities: whether public resources should continue sustaining an expanding weapons industry or be redirected toward meeting human needs. Building Solidarity Beyond Veterans' Organizations The panel also examined differences between traditional veterans' service organizations and newer advocacy groups such as Common Defense. Organizations including the American Legion and Veterans of Foreign Wars have historically played important roles in securing benefits and helping veterans navigate complicated claims processes. But traditional organizations have often avoided more confrontational political advocacy. Common Defense operates through nonprofit and political structures that allow it to participate more directly in campaigns, elections, and public policy debates. Goepel argued that veterans' credibility across political and geographic divisions gives them an unusual opportunity to communicate with communities that progressive organizations sometimes struggle to reach. That credibility, however, must be used to build solidarity rather than simply advance the interests of veterans alone. Related: When Workplace Organizing Gets Tough, Here’s How to Keep Going From Defending Institutions to Building Collective Power The larger message emerging from the Left Coast Forum discussion was that defending the VA cannot be separated from defending organized labor, public healthcare, and democratic accountability. The attacks on federal workers, the privatization of essential services, and the concentration of economic power are interconnected. So must be the response. Early and Goepel offered a vision of veterans not merely as recipients of government benefits or symbols of military service, but as workers, organizers, and advocates capable of helping build a broader movement. Their challenge to organized labor was equally clear: stop overlooking the veterans already within union ranks. And their challenge to the country was more ambitious. If Americans can establish public institutions to provide healthcare, education, and economic security for those who served in uniform, why should those same commitments to human dignity remain beyond reach for everyone else?
